newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Porsche profits soar to 6-yr high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Porsche profits soar to 6-yr high.

text.p: German sportscar maker Porsche AG, making a clear statement about its return to financial health, reported its highest net profit in six years on Friday.
It made a staggering 2,190 percent gain to 48 million marks ($31.78 million) for the 1995/96 business year to end-July.

Although the absolute profit level is not great for a company its size, the earnings enabled Porsche to pay its first preferred dividend since 1991/92, 2.50 marks, and vindicated predictions of contined sharp profit growth in 1996/97.

"This is evidence that Porsche is breaking through to a period of much higher profits," said Christopher Will, auto industry analyst at Lehman Brothers in London. "It's real evidence of an improved strategy."

Last year's earnings were the highest since 1989/90 when it made 57 million marks and marked the biggest step yet of a comeback since the company lost 238.8 million marks in 1992/93 and nearly went out of business.

Analysts said the profit figure, which was much greater than even Porsche had forecast as recently as several months ago, might have been larger, but that the car maker has traditionally followed very conservative accounting procedures.

The surge in profits came entirely on the back of Porsche's legendary 911 model -- a 30-year old design which the company has constantly updated and produced a record 20,100 of during the 1995/96 business year.
Analysts attributed the strong 911 sales to an attractive range of configurations of the car, strong economic growth and demand for luxury cars, especially in the U.S, Porsche's largest market.
"We have seen continued strong demand for the 911," said Lothar Lubinetski, analyst at Enskilda Corporate. "It just keeps selling."

Sweeping cost cutting in recent years has contributed to the other side of the profit equation. Porsche claims that it has slashed the time it takes to produce one of its Carrera models to 70 hours from 120 hours in 1992/93.

Analysts said after this year's sharp gain, Porsche's profit could soar to maybe 80 million marks in the current business year and likely well over 100 million marks next year as Porsche's new Boxster model hits the market.

The two-seat cabriolet, Porsche's first new car in nearly two decades, has won rave reviews from the motoring press and analysts, contributing to orders with dealers already equal to about a year's production.

Porsche figures demand for the car will lift production this year to near full capacity at 30,000 cars. And unlike the 911, which is considered a difficult car to make, the Boxster was made with production costs in mind, giving Porsche a wide profit margin.
The new model, which first went on sale in October, will not be fully felt in this business year's results, dampening its impact on the bottom line, analysts said.
Moreover, Porsche will start depreciating tool-up costs for the car this year, casting a question mark over just how large profits will be.
But analysts are in broad agreement that Porsche's profits should continue to climb.
"We will have to see the profit and loss statement, but Porsche should see a strong increase in profits again this year," Lubinetski said.
